notes: Every caption has a stable ID. A recorded voice line can later be added as audio/<id>.mp3 and will play with the caption. {name}-style tokens are filled in by the game. {key:action} and {hold:action} show the player's own key for an action on screen, in brackets, and are left out of narration (see src/input/bindings.ts).

captions.egg.intro: An egg in the gravel. There is little an egg can do but wait. Cold water seeps between the stones.
captions.egg.hatch: Hatched. The alevin lives on its yolk sac, hidden in the gravel. Alevin turn to face into the current: it keeps them upright and keeps oxygen-rich water flowing over their gills.
captions.egg.flow: The flow is shifting. Turn to face into the current {key:steer} before it surges.
captions.egg.loosening: The current is working you loose. Face upstream and sink deeper into the gravel {key:dive}.
captions.egg.ready: The yolk is nearly gone. Swim up toward the light {hold:rise} and out of the gravel, ready to feed.
captions.egg.emerge: The fry wriggles up out of the stones and into open water. Only about 10 to 20 percent of eggs get this far.
captions.fry.intro: The lake. Most sockeye spend one year here, some two, feeding on zooplankton.
captions.fry.controls: Click the water to steer with the mouse. Swim forward {key:forward}, burst {key:burst}, rise {key:rise} and dive {key:dive}. Swim through the glowing plankton to feed.
captions.fry.trout: A Dolly Varden has seen you. Rings in the water warn of a chase. The weeds at the shallow edge give cover.
captions.fry.safeWeeds: Hidden in the weeds. The Dolly Varden loses interest.
captions.fry.winter: Winter comes. Under the ice the fry grows slowly. Only about 5 to 10 percent of fry survive to leave the lake.
captions.smolt.intro: Spring. The young fish turns silver and leaves the lake at night, with thousands of others. Going together swamps the predators: they cannot eat everyone. Stay with the school.
captions.smolt.char: Char wait at the lake outlet. Rings in the water warn of a lunge. In a school, the char may take another fish instead of you.
captions.smolt.bird: A shadow on the surface: a diving bird. Go deep, or hide under the overhanging banks.
captions.smolt.merganser: A splash ahead: a merganser diving. It will chase underwater for a few seconds. Burst away.
captions.smolt.mouth: The river mouth and the first salt water. Gulls gather overhead and seals hunt the channel.
captions.smolt.gulls: Gulls, several at once. Watch every shadow.
captions.smolt.seal: Bubbles and a dark shape in the deep water: a seal. It will lunge straight. Swim across its path.
captions.smolt.alone: You've left the school. A lone fish is the predators' only choice.
captions.smolt.salt: The estuary. Of the {total} smolts that left the lake beside you, {lost} were taken. Since it turned silver, its gills and kidneys have been readying it for salt water.
captions.ocean.intro: The North Pacific. Sockeye stay in the top 20 to 40 metres and do most of their growing here. Feed where the krill and small fish gather.
captions.ocean.orca: A dark shape at the edge of sight: an orca. It will charge in a straight line. Swim across its path, not away from it.
captions.ocean.revealJack: Something has changed. This male is maturing early, after a single year at sea. He will return small, about 300 millimetres: a jack. Jacks are rare: in a typical Bristol Bay run only 1 or 2 males in 100 do this.
captions.ocean.revealLarge: {years} years at sea in all. This male will return large, with a hooked jaw, big teeth and a hump.
captions.ocean.revealFemale: After {years} years at sea, she turns for home.
captions.return.intro: Coming home from the open sea. Nearing the coast, the salmon stops eating and lives on what it has stored.
captions.return.fatHint: The fat bar is all the fuel left for this life. Bursting burns it fast.
captions.return.netSlip: Small enough to slip through the mesh. Gillnets catch many returning sockeye, especially the larger males whose heads and teeth tangle, but jacks often slip through.
captions.return.pastNets: Past the nets. Find the river mouth that smells like home.
captions.return.bear: A shadow and a splash at the bank: a bear. Shallow riffles are where bears fish. Wait in a pool, or cross deep and fast.
captions.return.lowFat: Reserves are running low. Rest in the slower water near the banks.
captions.return.wrongBranch: The scent is fading. This branch is not home: back out and try the other.
captions.spawn.female: Judge the gravel by its cobble: too coarse is hard to dig, too fine and the eggs get less oxygen. Dig the redd {hold:act}, wait over it for a male, then cover the eggs {hold:act}. Drive off rival females with a burst {key:burst}.
captions.spawn.largeMale: Stay beside the female. When a rival comes, ram him side-on with a burst {key:burst} before he reaches her. Fights are quick, and size usually wins.
captions.spawn.jack: You are too small to fight. Settle into a hiding spot under the bank. When the big males clash, dart in beside the female {key:act}.
captions.spawn.digging: Digging. Sweeps of the tail lift the gravel and the current carries the fine silt away.
captions.spawn.needGravel: This spot is no good. Look for gravel of medium cobble.
captions.spawn.rivalFemale: Another female wants this spot. Charge her with a burst {key:burst}.
captions.spawn.rivalMale: A rival male is moving in. Ram him side-on with a burst {key:burst} before he reaches her.
captions.spawn.reddDisturbed: A rival dug into your redd.
captions.spawn.maleLost: A rival reached the female while you were away.
captions.spawn.femaleSpawned: The male joins you over the redd. The eggs are laid and fertilized.
captions.spawn.maleSpawned: The female releases her eggs and you fertilize them.
captions.spawn.jackWindow: The big males are fighting. Now!
captions.spawn.jackSuccess: In and out before the guard noticed. Sneakers can fertilize some of the eggs, though usually fewer than a guarding male.
captions.spawn.jackChased: The guarding male drove you off. Wait for an opening.
captions.death.yolk: The yolk ran out before the alevin left the gravel. An alevin has to swim up and start feeding before its stored food is gone.
captions.death.scour: Washed out. A surge of water tore the alevin from the gravel. High flows that scour the gravel kill many eggs and alevin before they ever emerge.
captions.death.trout: Taken by a Dolly Varden. Trout and Dolly Varden are the main predators of fry in the lake.
captions.death.bird: Taken by a diving bird. Smolts near the surface are easy targets for mergansers and gulls.
captions.death.char: Taken by a char at the lake outlet. Larger fish gather where the smolts leave the lake.
captions.death.merganser: Taken by a merganser. These diving ducks chase smolts underwater.
captions.death.seal: Taken by a seal. Seals gather at river mouths when the smolts run, and hunt salmon throughout their years at sea.
captions.death.gillnet: Caught in a gillnet. The fish swims in, its head and teeth tangle, and it cannot back out. Larger males are caught most.
captions.death.bear: Taken by a bear. Bears feed most easily in shallow creeks. They take males first, then large females.
captions.death.exhaustion: Exhausted. Returning salmon do not eat, and this one ran out of stored energy before reaching home.
captions.death.noSpawn: Spawning failed. The season ended before this fish could spawn.
captions.end.decay: Like other Pacific salmon, a sockeye dies after spawning.
captions.end.forest: Its body feeds the stream, the insects, the bears and the trees along the bank.
captions.end.hatch: Under the gravel, the next generation is already growing.
captions.end.spentFemale: Spent, she guards the redd for as long as she can. Females live several weeks after spawning, rarely more than a month.
captions.end.spentMale: Spawned out, he grows sluggish and ragged on the grounds.
captions.end.carcass: The body settles among the stones and slowly breaks down.
captions.end.seasons: Autumn turns to winter, and winter to spring.
captions.egg.tooEarly: Not yet. Higher in the gravel the surges hit harder. Rise when the yolk is nearly used.
captions.ocean.shark: A fast grey shape below: a salmon shark. It will strike in a straight line. Swim across its path.
captions.ocean.yearsAtSea: Each extra year at sea brings more growth, and more risk: perhaps half of fish survive each later year. Jacks avoid this by returning early.
captions.ocean.crowded: A crowded year at sea. Pink salmon are abundant every other year, and sockeye grow less when they compete for food.
captions.death.sea: Lost at sea during a later year: orcas, salmon sharks or seals. Perhaps half of fish survive each extra year. Jacks, returning after one year, skip this risk.
captions.return.heat: A warm, low-water year. Heat stress and low oxygen kill fish before they spawn. Rest in the deeper, cooler pools.
captions.return.track: At sea, salmon navigate by the Earth's magnetic field. Feel for it: faint shimmering marks appear ahead when you are on the track. If they fade, sweep side to side until you find them again.
captions.return.lostTrack: The pull has faded. You've drifted off the track. Sweep across until the shimmer returns.
captions.return.overshoot: The coast. This doesn't feel like the right mouth. Overshooting is one of the commonest mistakes; turn back along the shore.
captions.return.wrongRiver: This river doesn't smell like home. Salmon test a river and back out when it is wrong. Turn around.
captions.return.rightRiver: The smell of home. This is the river.
captions.spawn.cobbleLarge: Coarse cobble. It is hard work to dig, and the redd will be poor.
captions.spawn.cobbleSmall: Fine gravel. Easy to dig, but the eggs will get less oxygen.
captions.spawn.fightWonSide: Side-on, mouth open: he gave way. Size usually wins, but timing and position helped.
captions.spawn.fightLost: He was bigger, and you were driven off. Hit rivals side-on, before they reach her.
captions.spawn.bear: A bear wades into the shallows. Bears take the biggest males first, then large females, and small jacks last. Watch for its shadow.
captions.spawn.bearTookGuard: The bear took the guarding male.
captions.spawn.jackScarce: Too many jacks, too few hiding spots. They fight each other for the cover under the bank.
captions.spawn.jackSpotTaken: Another jack holds this hiding spot. Charge him out with a burst {key:burst}, or find another.
captions.spawn.jackSpotWon: You pushed him out of the spot.
captions.spawn.jackEvicted: Another jack pushed you out of your hiding spot.
captions.spawn.habitat.creek: A small creek: shallow water and undercut banks. Bears catch fish most easily in creeks, and the bank cover gives jacks places to hide.
captions.spawn.habitat.river: A river: deeper, faster water over coarse gravel. River sockeye are larger and deeper-bodied than creek fish, and bears find them harder to catch.
captions.spawn.habitat.beach: A lake beach: still water along the shore. Beach spawners are the largest and deepest-bodied sockeye. Bears catch fish less easily here than in creeks, and there are few places for jacks to hide.
captions.spawn.jackBeach: You are too small to fight. Hide behind a boulder, the only cover on the beach. When the big males clash, dart in beside the female {key:act}.
captions.spawn.reddReady: The redd is dug. Stay over it and wait for a male.
captions.spawn.maleArrives: A male has joined you. He stays close while you dig.
captions.spawn.femaleChoice: Two males fight beside your redd. Fights are quick and mostly settled by size, and you will spawn with the winner.
captions.spawn.waitMale: The redd is ready, but no male is beside it. Wait over it.
captions.spawn.bury: Now cover the eggs: sweep gravel over them with your tail {hold:act} over the redd.
captions.spawn.buried: The eggs are covered. Guard the redd against other females for as long as your strength lasts.
captions.spawn.superimposed: Another female dug into your redd, and some of your eggs were dug up. Drive rivals off with a burst {key:burst}.
captions.spawn.senescence: Your strength is fading, and here it will not come back. After weeks on the spawning grounds, salmon turn sluggish and ragged.
captions.spawn.spentFemale: Your strength is gone. You guarded the redd for as long as you could. Females live several weeks after spawning, rarely more than a month.
captions.spawn.spentMale: Your strength is gone. Like other Pacific salmon, a sockeye dies after spawning.
captions.spawn.spentJack: Your strength is gone, and the season is over.
captions.spawn.femaleReady: She is ready to spawn. Get beside her, now.
captions.spawn.secondFemale: A second female has started to dig farther along the bed. In the game you can go to her or stay with the first; leaving costs strength and draws more bears.
captions.spawn.maleLeaves: You leave her to look for another female.
captions.spawn.maleSpawnedAgain: The second female releases her eggs and you fertilize them.
captions.spawn.secondLost: She spawned with another male before you reached her.
captions.spawn.jackCommon: Many jacks on the grounds this year: in the game, more of them compete for every opening, and each sneak is worth less.
captions.spawn.jackRare: Few jacks on the grounds this year: in the game, less competition for the openings, and each sneak is worth more.
captions.year.warm: A warm year. This year favours early-run fish. Late-run fish burn more fat on the way home.
captions.year.highWater: High water. This year, early-run and deep-bodied fish struggle more against the flow.
captions.year.lowWater: Low water. This year, deep-bodied fish are easier for bears to reach in the shallows.
captions.year.bigRun: A big run. More big males crowd the spawning grounds: harder for large males, more fights and openings for jacks.
captions.year.smallRun: A small run. Fewer rivals on the spawning grounds, which suits large males and leaves jacks fewer openings.
captions.year.crowded: A crowded ocean. Fish grow less at sea and come home smaller.
captions.year.ordinary: An ordinary year. No trait has a clear advantage.
captions.year.betHedging: Every year favours different fish. Over many years, a population that keeps its variety does better than one that bets on a single strategy.
captions.lineage.traitDrift: Each panel shows the inherited part of a trait, averaged over the brood each fish was chosen from. Zero is the home population's average. The offspring you pick, the mates they meet, strays and chance all move it.
captions.lineage.extinct: The whole brood died before any of them could spawn. Nothing of this line returns to the gravel.
captions.lineage.strayOffer: Salmon sometimes stray from the stream they were born in. A stray that has joined this river can start a new line here.
captions.year.cool: A cool year. This year favours late-run fish, which burn less fat on the way home.
captions.return.angler: A flash in the pool: an angler's lure swinging across the current. Give it a wide berth.
captions.return.hooked: Hooked! Burst again and again {key:burst} to tear free before the line wins.
captions.return.unhooked: Free. The hook tore loose, but the fight cost precious fat.
captions.death.angler: Landed by an angler. Sport fishing takes returning salmon in the rivers, as the commercial nets do on the approach.
captions.fry.lesson: Early summer, at the weed edge. Watch for rings spreading through the water: they mean a Dolly Varden is about to chase. When you see them, dart into the weeds.
captions.fry.lessonDone: Well read. Food in the open is worth having, but only with cover close by.
captions.fry.dusk: Midsummer evenings. As the light fades, the plankton rises toward the surface. The richest feeding is up high, in open water, where Dolly Varden and trout hunt.
captions.fry.winterHint: The water is cold and food is scarce. Every burst spends reserves you cannot easily replace. Rest when you can: ease off {key:forward} and take only the food that drifts close.
captions.fry.starving: The reserves are gone, and the fry is burning its own growth to stay alive. Rest, and find food.
captions.fry.decide: About 6 in 10 sockeye leave the lake after one year. Follow the drifting current to the outlet to leave now, or wait in the weeds to stay another year: a bigger fish when it leaves, but another year among the predators.
captions.fry.decideGrown: This fry grew well this year.
captions.fry.decideSmall: This fry grew slowly this year. Another year in the lake would make it bigger when it leaves.
captions.fry.secondSummer: A second summer in the lake.
captions.fry.second: Bigger now, but the predators are still here. Feed at dusk, and keep the weeds close.
captions.fry.secondWinter: Another winter passes under the ice.
captions.fry.leave: After one year in the lake, like most sockeye, the young fish follows the current toward the outlet.
captions.fry.leaveSecond: After two years in the lake, a bigger young fish follows the current toward the outlet.
captions.ocean.skipOrca: Weeks later, farther out. Another patch of food, and something large is hunting here too.
captions.ocean.skipSeal: Feeding near the surface. Seals and sea lions hunt salmon throughout their years at sea.
captions.ocean.seal: Bubbles and a dark shape: a seal. It lunges at where you are going, so turn hard as it comes.
captions.ocean.pinks: Pink salmon everywhere, all after the same food. Get to it first.
captions.ocean.pinksGone: A lean season: less food for every fish.
captions.ocean.skipShark: Months pass. Deeper water, and something fast below.
captions.ocean.autumnMale: For a male, this is thought to be when his path is set. His genes, and how fast he has grown, decide whether he matures early.
